It should be curious and human, but still disciplined enough for a research audience.", "PALETTE: Use warm notebook white (#FFFDF7), deep blue ink (#17324D), teal (#0F766E), specimen yellow (#E6B84C), and pale teal wash (#D7E8E5). Use color as a coding system, not as decoration. Use the original palette with strong text/background contrast. Pale tints serve as surfaces, not low-contrast body text; differentiate critical states with wording or shape as well as color.", "TYPOGRAPHY: Use an exceptionally legible sans-serif for all core text. Reserve a subtle handwritten-style accent only for short diagram callouts; never use it for body text, data labels, or citations. Use an available Hangul-capable font for Korean labels and wrap long names at phrase boundaries. Keep equations in a dedicated text area with intact variables, units, subscripts, and superscripts; allow extra line height rather than shrinking below the runtime typography floor. At 1280x720, use the Korean-safe stack \"Noto Sans KR\", \"Malgun Gothic\", \"Apple SD Gothic Neo\", sans-serif for Korean text. Body text should normally be 22-28px; captions and source notes preferably at least 16px. The hard minimum for every visible text run is 9.5pt (12.667px). Recompose, shorten or split content before reducing readability; never shrink below this floor. Preserve any genre-specific display-face accents only where Korean fallback remains clear.", "LAYOUT SYSTEM: Set diagrams on an airy modular grid with a clear central process or specimen. Build explanations in numbered steps, leave room for labels, and maintain strong contrast between mark, background, and annotation. Reserve an outer safe margin, a label lane beside the specimen, and a separate observation/source band. Route leaders through clear space with explicit endpoints; move crowded callouts to a numbered key and keep calibration marks away from explanatory text. Build around one explanatory model with cleanly aligned evidence nearby. Let a few hand-drawn strokes reveal a mechanism or question while labels and plots remain precise. Alternate conceptual sketches, observations and experimental next steps; use open space to make relationships inspectable. These are free compositional choices driven by content, never fixed layouts or required slots. Give the main evidence generous space and vary visual density across the deck.", "SIGNATURE ELEMENTS: Include hand-drawn-style arrows, numbered callout circles, specimen labels, calibration ticks, light graph-paper fragments, and concise observation notes. Keep imperfect ink-like outlines on conceptual objects and use teal/yellow sparingly to direct attention. Reserve a distinct solid mark style for observed data so a sketched hypothesis cannot be mistaken for a measurement.", "DATA VISUALIZATION: Use explanatory plots, labeled process diagrams, simple before/ after comparisons, and small multiples. Label every variable, unit, condition, and sample when supplied; distinguish measured data from illustrative diagrams. Keep small-multiple axes and before/after conditions comparable. Draw measured curves from actual observations; hand-drawn accents must not shift data marks or axes. Calibration ticks require a known scale; omit decorative scales and do not invent samples, measurements, or equations to fill space. Label the boundary between hypothesis, observation and inference. Use straight axes and accurately placed points for measurements; hand-drawn arrows may express proposed mechanisms only when explicitly named. Mark simulated values and leave unknown magnitudes unknown.", "IMAGE DIRECTION: Use close-up specimens, field observations, microscope imagery, or technical line illustrations. Add thin annotation leaders and source captions without obscuring the subject.", "SLIDE ARCHETYPES: cover: one specimen or sketch with title and field-note label; content: a single concept diagram with a small set of source-supported numbered explanations, grouping dense steps without removing required information; data: a readable plot paired with a plain-language observation; timeline: experiment phases marked with supplied phases and explicit planned or completed status; section: one scientific question beside a small specimen sketch; agenda: an aligned list of the supplied questions with restrained numbered marks; architecture: a mechanism or experimental setup with labeled components and arrows in documented directions, leaving clear corridors between labels and distinguishing hypotheses from observed relationships; closing: a summary sketch that restates the mechanism and the open question. Additional forms: mechanism sketch beside observations; hypothesis-versus-result comparison; experiment sequence with a control; measured trend with an annotated anomaly; next-experiment proposal tied to one unresolved question.", "AVOID: Avoid childish doodles, low-contrast pencil effects, decorative equations, unlabeled arrows, crowded callouts, and treating an illustrative sketch as evidence.
